title: Kinetica: designing a racer around bodies built for speed
summary: Kinetica makes the racer and the vehicle one object: competitors wear powered suits that sprint, leap, and cling to curved track surfaces. Santa Monica Studio’s first PlayStation 2 game turns that premise into a readable arcade racer through broad track shapes, boost decisions, and a visual language that keeps the moving body visible against the course.
heroAlt: A motorcycle racer leaning into a turn on the race track.
author: EmuCore - Hub

blocks.text: A vehicle that can take the inside wall

Kinetica’s central image is also its handling thesis: the rider is inside a kinetic suit, not seated in a conventional car. Sony’s current listing describes suits that climb walls, perform acrobatics and reach extreme speed. That body-machine fusion lets the course bend vertically without asking the player to infer a separate vehicle’s orientation. The avatar stays legible as the track tilts, so the spectacle communicates where momentum is going.

The game’s courses use banked surfaces, loops and sweeping transitions to make route choice visible at speed. A turn is not just a test of steering precision; it can redirect the rider onto a wall or toward a jump. The player learns to read the track as a continuous ribbon and to anticipate how a curve will shape the next landing. This spatial grammar is what lets the game feel futuristic while keeping its basic objective familiar.

Power-ups and boost sections add a tactical layer to the race. Spending speed at the wrong moment can send a rider into a difficult landing or leave too little acceleration for a straight. The decision is therefore bound to the geometry, rather than being a button pressed whenever a meter allows it. Sony’s listing also calls out siphon boosts, shortcuts and drafting, which frame speed as something racers can create through positioning as well as collect.
Nine suits make identity part of the roster

The official store description advertises nine exclusive kinetic suits and more than twelve tracks. A suit roster gives the sport a visual cast and makes the impossible premise concrete: this is a competition with athletes and equipment, not anonymous vehicles on a science-fiction circuit. Track variety then supplies changing conditions for that cast. The combination makes selection and mastery part of the game’s appeal.

Released in North America on 18 October 2001, Kinetica was Santa Monica Studio’s first game. Its design compresses a memorable fiction, a readable course and a tight speed loop into one idea: bodies can race where cars cannot. The later PlayStation Store conversion identifies the original PS2 version and developer, while its feature list preserves the game’s emphasis on wall-running, acrobatics and track tactics.
